summary:
Workplace Insight argues there is an "AI utilisation gap": employees use AI more deeply and broadly in their personal lives than at work. Citing the 2026 annual WIN World AI Index (roughly 40,000 respondents across 44 countries), the piece reports global AI adoption at 74 percent, up from 62 percent a year earlier, with 39 percent of people intentionally using AI often or every day, signalling a shift from experimentation to habit.

Daily use is nearly level across contexts (12 percent personal versus 10 percent at work), but the composition differs sharply. Workplace use clusters in a narrow set of approved, productivity-linked activities: research and data analysis (38 percent of users) and workflow automation (28 percent). Personal use is far wider: entertainment (39 percent), schoolwork (32 percent) and content creation (31 percent), plus question answering, learning, ideation and everyday problem solving.

The author attributes the divergence to freedom versus control. At home people can experiment and learn by trial and error; at work AI arrives wrapped in governance frameworks, compliance requirements and approved use cases that, while necessary, may narrow exploration and limit confidence. The result is a workforce moving faster than the workplace, with employees treating AI as a thinking partner while organisations treat it as a task-specific tool.

The recommendation is to shift from adoption drives to enablement: governance without enablement leaves staff permitted but not empowered. Forward-thinking employers should stop asking where AI saves time and instead ask where it helps people make better decisions, solve complex problems and focus on higher-value work, using AI to rethink how work gets done rather than automating existing processes.

The piece notes a caveat from the index: trust in AI capability has improved while comfort has declined, meaning people are more confident in what AI can do but less certain about wider implications. If organisations fail to create enabling conditions, the gap between personal confidence and workplace application will widen.
